title: What the Road Was Cut For
logline: A road runs into the last large lowland rainforest on the island. It was cut, by one account, as a jeep track for scientists; it was widened for the heaviest logging machinery of its day to feed a plywood factory; after six years of a campaign against the logging it now carries researchers and walkers, past skid tracks that were planted afterwards with a foreign timber tree, as what foresters call enrichment, and that a later directory lists as a threat to the forest. Filmed entirely from the road, in monsoon rain, the film asks what the texts ask of effort: whether the work itself has any colour of its own.
human_question: If the same hard, unrelenting work can take a forest down, keep it standing, or try to mend it, is there anything in the work itself that says which of those I am doing?

place.what_kind_of_place: A lowland tropical rainforest in the wet south-west, on a narrow strip of steep ridges and valleys, protected under a law made for it alone and inscribed as a natural World Heritage site. The film uses one thing inside it: the old road that enters from the north-western edge and runs a few kilometres in to a clearing where a research station now stands. The road runs through the logged part of the forest. It is the way the machines came in and the timber went out in the 1970s, and it is the way almost every visitor walks in now. On either side, forest regrown over half a century; along the old skid tracks, an introduced timber tree planted afterwards (the payoff depends on finding a row of it still standing); beyond, the unlogged interior, which the camera does not enter.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Rain on a rainforest is one of the great sights and sounds on the island, and almost nobody films it, because everybody comes in the dry months. Here the south-west monsoon arrives as a roar on a canopy thirty or forty metres up before a drop reaches the ground; mist lifts off the ridges in the gaps; streams beside the road go brown and loud; leaves the size of a hand shed water in sheets. The road itself is a strong graphic object: a pale earth line running into dark forest, framed so that it always vanishes in the middle distance. With the sound off the film is a walk-in that never walks: a sequence of held frames down one road in the rain, from the forest seen far off under cloud to the clearing where the road stops.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Only water and weather. The rain comes and goes in bands; the light under the canopy changes from dark green to almost black and back; the mist moves; the streams rise. Mixed flocks of forest birds cross the road when the rain eases, and that is luck. The camera never moves: every shot is locked on a tripod on the road's own line. People who pass (guides, researchers, walkers) are small figures at the far end of a long frame and never faces.
place.when_it_looks_best: The south-west monsoon, roughly May to July, which the protected-areas directory gives as the main rains; mornings, when bands of rain alternate with lifting mist. The dry month (February in the same directory) is the wrong season for this film. A day of steady rain followed by a break is ideal: the break gives the payoff frame its light.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A rain film on one road into a rainforest. It opens on the forest far off, ridges under cloud, seen from outside its edge. Then it goes in by the road and never leaves it: held frames looking straight down the road's line, the vanishing point always in the middle of the frame, rain in every shot, the sound of water on leaves carrying the whole piece. Near the end the road reaches a clearing and stops. The last frame is the only one in the film not composed down the road: the camera turns square to the roadside and holds on a row of tall straight trunks all of one kind, standing in a line among the forest's crooked, various trees, while the rain eases off. It is a complete piece about entering a forest in the wet.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same road becomes the demonstration of C021's central finding: the occasional factors, effort among them, are found in good and bad minds alike and take the moral quality of the mind they join. The road has carried three efforts: a track for scientists, a haul road for logging machinery, a way in for research and for visitors. The voice names each from the written record and says, with the Margaya, that the bodily and mechanical strength that moved the logs is not what the texts mean by effort at all. It gives the Pradeepika's image of effort in a mind already leaning one way, a boat on water running downhill, and good done like a load carried uphill, and refuses to hang that image on anyone here: both the logging contract and the campaign against it ran for years. C005 enters once, to say what the texts would need in order to judge the logging, the aim, and that the record holds a stated use and not a mind. The payoff is the planted row: a valuable timber put back, as 'enrichment', along the lines the extraction cut, and later itself listed as a threat. Nothing in the frame is good or bad; the texts put that in the mind, where no camera goes.

sequence.on_screen: From outside the forest's edge, on the road below the entrance, a long lens across tea and scrub to forested ridges under low monsoon cloud. Rain crossing the ridges in grey bands. Locked. Nearly a minute before anything else happens.
sequence.voice: This is the largest stretch of lowland rainforest left on the island. Most of it was declared a forest reserve in 1875, and in 1936 a visiting biologist called it the only considerable patch of virgin rain forest the island still had. It was hard to reach and steep, and the record says it remained untouched. In 1968 a government directive changed that: its trees were to feed a new plywood and chipboard factory.

sequence.on_screen: Inside the entrance. The camera on the crown of the road, looking straight along it: pale earth, puddles, the road running into dark forest and vanishing in the middle of the frame. Rain. Held.
sequence.voice: This road is the way in. One account says it was first cut in 1963, as a jeep track for scientists. The campaign's own history says that contractors on a foreign-aided logging contract cleared a wide road here, wide enough to haul in the heaviest extraction machinery of the day and to take the timber out by lorry. Both accounts start from the same village north of the forest, and both are describing the way in. The texts in this series name six factors that turn up in some minds and not in others, and say that each is wholly good in a good mind and wholly bad in a bad one. None of them has a colour of its own.

sequence.on_screen: Further in. The same axial frame on a stretch where the road is sunk between banks and roots, water running down its ruts in two brown threads. A wide drip line from the canopy edge. Held.
sequence.voice: One of the six is effort: in the Margaya's words, the nature of not falling back from a task, of going on until what was begun is done. The Margaya is careful here. Bodily strength is also called effort, it says, but that is not what is meant; bodily strength is not a factor of mind at all. Whatever dragged logs down this road was strength. The thing the texts mean is what kept a contract going, and what kept the opposition to it going, and the road does not record it.

sequence.on_screen: A stream beside the road in spate: a locked frame at the water's edge, brown water racing downhill over rock, rain dimpling the eddies.
sequence.voice: The Pradeepika gives effort an image. In a mind already leaning towards harm, effort carries it along easily, like a boat on water flowing downhill. Doing good means working against that, like a man carrying a load up a hill, and without effort it cannot be done at all. It is an image of a mind. It does not say which side of any quarrel is the downhill one, and nothing here does either. By the directory of the island's protected areas, the logging ran from 1971 to 1977; another account has it stopping in 1972 and starting again in 1974. The opposition ran as long.

sequence.on_screen: Back on the road, axial frame at a bend where the canopy closes overhead and the road goes almost dark. A band of heavy rain arrives: first the sound high up, then, seconds later, the drops on the road. Held through it.
sequence.voice: In 1970 a society of naturalists had agreed to the logging, provided a small block was spared. In 1972, led by its president, Thilo Hoffmann, it turned against it entirely: a booklet in two languages, a memorandum to the Prime Minister signed by many other bodies, years of hearings before a government committee. By the Forest Department's own figures, about fourteen hundred hectares of this western sector had been selectively logged when it stopped. A figure ten times that is repeated in print, in what looks like a copy of the same sentence with one digit added; it is bigger than the whole reserve.

sequence.on_screen: The road coming out into a clearing: grass, a low building set back among trees, the forest wall behind. The camera stays on the road's line, at the point where the road stops. Rain easing.
sequence.voice: Both sides wrote down a reason, and both reasons were the nation's interest: timber and self-sufficiency on one side, an irreplaceable forest on the other. The Margaya lists earning, acquiring and guarding wealth among the ordinary occasions when wanting mostly arises, and says the same earning, done with wisdom placed foremost and an eye to what is useful, raises no unwholesome mind. It sorts the act by its aim. A contract states a use. It does not state a mind, and the texts give nobody the means to read one off a road.

sequence.on_screen: Still at the clearing, looking along the road's last few metres into it. Mist lifting off the trees behind. A mixed flock of small birds crosses the road if the break in the rain gives one; if not, the drip and the mist only.
sequence.voice: By the campaign's account, a machine yard and a repair shop once stood where the research station stands today, the ground soaked with fuel. The texts' word for the wish to do is chanda: the wish to take something up, which, they insist, is not the force that makes a mind stick. Beside greed it feeds greed. Beside a good mind it works against greed, and trained, it carries a mind as far as the texts go. Whoever came in here, and for whatever reason, the texts would give the wish to come in the same name.

sequence.on_screen: The one frame not composed down the road. The camera turns square to the roadside and holds on a row of tall, straight, grey-barked trunks all of one kind, standing in a line among the forest's crooked, mixed trees. The rain stops. Water keeps falling from the leaves for a long time. Hold to the end.
sequence.voice: The machines' skid tracks were planted afterwards with mahogany, a timber tree from the other side of the world, as what foresters call enrichment: a valuable timber put back into logged ground. The campaign itself had proposed mahogany to enrich degraded forest elsewhere. A later directory of the island's protected areas lists it among this forest's problems: it seeds so freely it may crowd out the forest's own trees. A planting, laid on the same line as the taking. The Pradeepika says effort, grown strong, can carry a mind all the way to awakening. It never says that effort, by itself, is good. This row is the straightest thing in the forest.

concept_merge.why_together: C021 is primary and carries the film. Its governing finding is that the six occasional factors are found in both beautiful and unbeautiful minds and are counted wholly wholesome with wholesome minds and wholly unwholesome with unwholesome ones [C021-P:L25]. Of the six, this film takes effort, which no other film in the group builds on: the Margaya defines it as not falling back from a task until what was begun is done, and separates it explicitly from bodily strength, which it says is not a mental factor [C021-M:L19]; the Pradeepika gives the downhill boat and the uphill load, and says strong effort developed as a perfection can reach awakening [C021-P:L53]. Desire-to-act enters once, as the wish to take up an object that is not itself sticking and runs with or against greed according to the mind it joins [C021-P:L75] [C021-M:L27]. C005 is supporting and has one job: to name what the texts would need to judge the logging, the aim, and to show that the record does not contain it. It lists earning, acquiring and guarding wealth among the occasions when greed-rooted minds mostly arise [C005-M:L5], and exempts the same acts when faith, kindness or compassion is placed foremost, or wisdom with regard to usefulness [C005-M:L9].
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: Together they stop the film becoming the story it most wants to be, a forest saved by the good from the greedy. C021 says the effort on both sides is the same factor and that its moral colour is supplied by a mind; C005 says the logging would be sorted by its aim, and the only aim in writing is a stated national use, which the texts treat as the exempt case if it was truly foremost and as an occasion of wanting if it was not. The camera can show neither. What it can show is one road that three efforts used in turn, and a row of timber trees planted along the skid tracks as enrichment, which a later directory names as a hazard: effort laid on the same line, carrying no guarantee of its own.

concept_links.why: The Pradeepika says the six occasional factors occur in both beautiful and unbeautiful minds, sometimes present and sometimes not, and are wholly wholesome with wholesome minds and wholly unwholesome with unwholesome ones [C021-P:L25]. This road's written history is that sentence on the ground: one line cut, by the accounts, for science, widened for logging machinery, and used now for research and for visitors, with the forest's regrowth and an enrichment planting of mahogany along it. The film builds on effort. The Margaya defines it as the nature of not falling back from a task and going forward until what was begun is done, and says bodily strength, also called effort, is not a mental factor [C021-M:L19]; the machinery that worked here is strength, and the texts' effort is the thing no road records. The Pradeepika's image is of a worldling's mind bent towards evil in which effort goes easily to the unwholesome side, like a boat on water flowing downward, while good must be done with effort, like carrying a load up a hill; it adds that strong effort, practised as a perfection, can reach awakening [C021-P:L53]. The film gives that image as an image of a mind and explicitly refuses to assign the downhill to either side of the logging dispute. Desire-to-act is the wish to take up the object, not the force that makes the mind stick [C021-P:L69]; in greed-rooted minds it supports greed, in wholesome minds it helps suppress it, and developed it helps overcome craving [C021-P:L75] [C021-M:L27]. The digest's does_not_transfer lines are the film's guards: 'Hard work is always virtuous' is refused (effort is neutral and can power harm as easily as good), so the campaign is not narrated as virtuous effort; 'Desire is the enemy' is refused, so the wish to go into the forest, the scientists', the loggers', the visitors', is not condemned; 'Follow your passion' is refused, so the campaign's persistence is not offered as proof it was right.

The Margaya lists, among the ordinary occasions on which greed-rooted minds mostly arise, doing many things to earn wealth, acquiring it and guarding what has been acquired [C005-M:L5]; and it says that earning, guarding and spending wealth done with faith, loving-kindness or compassion placed foremost, or with wisdom placed foremost with regard to usefulness, raises no unwholesome mind [C005-M:L9]. The logging of this forest is the case the rule was written for: a state enterprise extracting timber for a factory, under a stated reason of national need for timber and self-sufficiency. Ruling, made on reading the source lines: undecidable. The exemption in C005-M:L9 turns on what is placed foremost in the mind, and no document here reaches a mind; the stated reason is a sentence in a plan and a committee report, not an aim anyone can inspect. The film therefore says the texts would sort the act by its aim and that the record does not hold it, and it neither exempts the logging nor convicts it. It follows the digest's does_not_transfer: 'Only intentions matter' is not said (the source still names particular harmful actions, and the film does not dissolve the damage into motive: the damage is filmed and figured); 'minimalism' or 'self-denial is virtue' is not said, since the source allows wealth earned and spent wisely. The digest notes that the M:L9 cases are called 'not unwholesome' without saying what they are instead; the film never calls any act here wholesome.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the drive to get something done, pushing on, refusing to give up, is not good or bad by itself, and that the same road can carry it in any direction. The proof on screen needs no belief: one road, documented as a scientists' track, a logging haul road and now a research and visitors' route; a row of timber trees planted along the logging tracks as 'enrichment' and later named a threat. And, from C005, that the texts judge acts like logging by their aim, and that an honest film has to say it cannot see the aim.
what_must_be_real: The road, the rain, the streams, the mist and the planted row as found. Nothing staged: no one asked to walk the road for the camera, no birds called or baited, no leaves sprayed. Guides, researchers and visitors appear, if at all, as small unrecognisable figures at the far end of a long frame; no face, no named worker, no villager, no forest officer is framed. No logger, contractor, official or campaigner is shown or narrated as wanting, greedy, zealous or right: the voice gives what was done and what was written, and where each account comes from. Every figure in the voice is the one the record gives, with its source, and the variant 14,000-hectare figure is named as an error, never used. The payoff row must actually be mahogany planted on an old skid track and visible from the road; if it cannot be found and identified on the ground with the Forest Department, the beat is dropped rather than faked with another row.
position_hint: Mid-group in GRP-02, after a film that establishes that the drive under any wanting has no colour of its own (the shooting-ground film) and not adjacent to it: this is the film that tests that finding on effort specifically and on a case where the obvious verdict is moral. It works well just before the films about one act with two aims, because it ends by handing C005's question (what was the aim?) to them unanswered.
risks: Turning into a hero story. The campaign's history reaches us mainly through the campaigner's authorised biography and the society's own journal, which are interested parties; the other side's main document, the government committee's report published in 1976, was reached only through quotations in that biography. The voice names the campaign's acts and says whose account the details come from, and gives the logging side's stated reason in its own terms.

Framing any identifiable person as wanting or as virtuous. Floor for GRP-02: no logger, contractor, official, politician or campaigner is narrated as greedy, zealous or right. Thilo Hoffmann is named for his documented acts only. No politician is named in the voice.

'Hard work is always virtuous' (C021 does_not_transfer): the campaign's persistence must not be offered as its justification, and the downhill boat must never be pinned on the logging or the uphill load on the campaign. The voice says explicitly that the image is of a mind and that nothing here says which side was downhill.
'Desire is the enemy' (C021 does_not_transfer): the wish to go into the forest, whoever's, is not condemned; the film ends on desire-to-act as the texts describe it, capable of either direction.

C005 overreach: 'Only intentions matter' is not said, and no act is called wholesome (the digest notes that the M:L9 exemptions are 'not unwholesome' without further classification). The ruling is undecidable and the voice says the aim is not in the record.

Living community. People live and work on the forest's edge and some depend on its produce; the directory records resettlement plans. None of this enters the film: no villager, no house, no kitul tapping, no minor forest produce, no statement about local use. The 1936 biologist's remarks about the villagers' veneration of the forest are not used.

Live institutional dispute. The campaigner's memoir accuses the Forest Department, which now manages the reserve, of having pressed for the logging and of making its own law to keep control of the forest. That rivalry is not entered in the voice; the film uses the department's own published figures and the independent directory.

Repetition in the group. The shooting-ground film (IDEA-0019) is the other C021-primary film on protected wild land and deliberately left the campaign story, the boat image and the society's later names to this film; this film does not use its long-lens-from-a-vehicle method, its animals or its reverse angle. The garden film (IDEA-0020) walks one unbroken take and builds on the Margaya's line on initial application and on 'the record gives the acts, not the mind'; this film never walks, uses effort rather than initial application, and does not use that refrain. The church film (IDEA-0017) uses decision (C021-P:L45); this film does not.

Archetype. A protected forest is on the slate (a montane strict nature reserve, IDEA-0143; montane restoration plots in a conservation forest, IDEA-0062; a forest hermitage in a forest reserve, IDEA-0121) and felling is on the slate twice (a plantation block, IDEA-0136; a home-garden tree, IDEA-0185). None is a timber concession halted by a campaign, and none is filmed from one road in rain; the overlap of kind is stated, not hidden.

Treatment overlap with the frost film (IDEA-0013), whose payoff is also a change of weather in a held frame. Here the payoff is a change of axis (the only off-road frame) onto a planted object; the easing rain is incidental and the shot works in rain as well.
Leeches, rain on the lens, low light under the canopy. The film depends on shooting in the wet; a camera kept dry only in dry spells will not make it.
drop_if: The Forest Department will not permit tripod filming on the road during the south-west monsoon.

No planted mahogany row can be found and identified from the road with the department's help; in that case the payoff is rebuilt on the research-station clearing alone, and if that is too thin the film is refused rather than padded.

The machine-yard claim for the research-station ground cannot be confirmed with the department or another source independent of the campaign's biography; the beat is then rewritten to say only that the account comes from one side.
The film cannot be made without a living community or a named worker becoming its subject.

connections.note: The other C021-primary film in GRP-02, on a former sportsmen's shooting ground that became a national park, whose history comes largely from the same naturalists' society. That film left the campaign story, the downhill-boat image and the society's later names to this one. It is dry-season heat haze through a very long lens from a halted vehicle, with animals and a reverse angle onto the camera; this is monsoon rain on foot-level tripod frames down one road, with no animal subject and a payoff on a planted row.

A designed garden made by clearing and planting over half a century, on C021's desire-to-act and initial application. It is one unbroken walking take that stops where the garden stops. This film does not move at all, builds on effort rather than initial application, and ends on planting done to repair rather than to compose a view.

A pilgrimage church on sand whose founding tellings place faith and prosperity differently; it carries C005's 'placed foremost' ruling and C021's decision factor at noon under a banyan. This film leaves decision to it and uses C005 only to say the aim is not in the record.

selection.reason: Kept on the blind GRP-02 selection's proposal after testing both halves, with its story rebuilt and several of its facts corrected. The story half is stronger than the proposal knew: beyond the logging and the campaign, the written record gives one road that three efforts used in turn (a scientists' jeep track by one account, a logging haul road, a research and visitors' route), a logging machine yard on the ground where a research station now stands (by the campaign's account), and skid tracks planted with mahogany as an 'enrichment species' that the protected-areas directory of 1990 then lists as a threat. That is C021's colourless effort in documents, not by analogy. The disputed area figure was resolved: 1,400 ha is the Forest Department's and Gunatilleke's figure as carried by the IUCN directory of 1990; 14,000 ha is a copying error in a later reproduction of the same sentence and is larger than the whole reserve. The picture half holds in the monsoon, which is when almost nobody films here. The proposal's treatment (drone along the western edge, handheld walk along the track) was replaced because walking repeats IDEA-0020 and a drone in a World Heritage forest is both the cliché and unlikely to be permitted.

review.note:
This record's body was replaced in full on 2026-09-26 in the blind GRP-02 re-selection, written without reading the previous body. The previous status was already pending, so no confirmation or rejection has been reset, but under standing decision 9 any earlier reading of this record no longer applies. The concepts are unchanged (C021 primary, C005 supporting). The location, proposed by Claude and not yet reviewed by Chathura, is the old logging road into the north-western sector of the lowland rainforest reserve, entered from its main entrance, running to the research-station clearing (its district moves from 2 to 3 films with this one, counting only the films currently written). It was the blind selection's proposal, tested and kept with its story rebuilt round the road. Corrected or held apart: the logged area (1,400 ha in the IUCN directory of 1990, citing Gunatilleke 1978 and the Forest Department 1986, against 14,000 ha in a National Trust Sri Lanka leaflet that reproduces the directory's sentence word for word with one digit added; the larger figure exceeds the reserve's entire area and is recorded as an error, never averaged); the aid behind the project (the plywood complex built with Romanian aid and the logging contract with Canadian aid, per the campaigner's authorised biography; a 2015 review in the Sunday Times says the factory itself was Canadian-built, a conflation); the end of logging (1977 in the directory, 1978 in the same review, and a stop in 1972 with a restart in 1974 in Ishwaran and Erdelen 1990 as cited); and the campaigner's own later dates for the protecting law (1985) and the declaration (1989), which the Act's number (No. 3 of 1988) and the gazette of 21 October 1988 contradict. The treatment was changed from the proposal's drone and handheld walk to locked tripod frames down the road's axis in monsoon rain, with no drone. C005's exemption was ruled undecidable. The weakest points are that the campaign's detail comes mainly from the campaigner's side, that the machine-yard ground and the visibility of a planted row from the road are unconfirmed, and that protected forest is a kind of place already on the slate.

Audit 2026-09-26: independent second check against the IUCN directory (1990) and the Island excerpt of the Hoffmann biography. Changed: (1) the mahogany payoff no longer says the planting was made 'to repair' or 'mend' the logging damage; no source says so. The directory calls it planting 'as an enrichment species' (valuable timber put into logged forest) and the biography gives no reason; the logline, two_layers, beat 8, concept_merge, the C021 link, why_here, how_it_binds, what_the_viewer_could_understand and the selection reason were corrected, and beat 8 now adds, from the biography, that Hoffmann himself proposed mahogany enrichment of degraded forest elsewhere in June 1972. The '1987 review' warning is now attributed to the 1990 directory, which is where it was read (citing de Zoysa and Raheem 1987). (2) Beat 5 said the society argued against the logging 'from 1971'; the biography has it agreeing to the logging in 1970 if 1,000 to 1,200 acres were spared, and turning against it only in 1972; corrected. (3) Beat 4 stated Ishwaran and Erdelen's stop-and-restart dates as fact; the directory's 1971 to 1977 is now given first and the variant as another account. (4) Beat 2's 'It is the same line on the ground' overclaimed: the 1963 track and the contractors' road are both described only as running from Veddagala; softened. (5) Beat 7 no longer places the machine yard 'where the road ends'; the source says 'where the Research Station stands today'. (6) The connection to IDEA-0026 and the district-count references to its proposed film were removed, since that slot was reopened. Still unverified: whether a planted mahogany row survives and is visible from the road; which building the biography means by the research station; the 1963 jeep track in its original; everything on the ground. The strongest objection stands: the campaign's detail comes mainly from the campaigner's authorised biography, and the payoff depends on a row nobody has confirmed.

suggested_location.name: Sinharaja Forest Reserve (Sinharaja National Heritage Wilderness Area): the old logging road from the Kudawa entrance to the Kudawa research-station clearing, north-western sector

also_known_as.name: Sinharaja
also_known_as.meaning: commonly glossed 'lion king'; the IUCN directory (1990) reports readings as a royal forest of the Sinhalese or the home of a legendary lion

also_known_as.name: Sinharaja National Heritage Wilderness Area
also_known_as.meaning: its designation under the National Heritage Wilderness Areas Act No. 3 of 1988

also_known_as.name: Kudawa (also Weddagala / Veddagala side)
also_known_as.meaning: the village at the main north-western entrance, and the village north of it named in accounts of the first road

suggested_location.region: Ratnapura District, Sabaragamuwa Province (Kalawana area). The reserve as a whole spans Ratnapura, Galle and Matara districts; the entrance village (6.4404, 80.4208) and the research-station clearing (OpenStreetMap 'Kudawa Research Centre', 6.4168, 80.4237) both reverse-geocode to Ratnapura District on OpenStreetMap/Nominatim, and the IUCN directory places the reserve office at Kudawa, Weddagala. Every shot in the film is on this stretch.
suggested_location.why_here: The primary concept needs an effort that is visibly the same thing whatever it serves. Here that is not an analogy but a road: the one route into the north-western sector, which the record describes as cut for scientists, widened for logging machinery, and now used for research and by almost every visitor, running through exactly the part of the forest that was logged, past skid tracks planted afterwards with an introduced timber tree as an 'enrichment species'. The logging and the campaign that stopped it were both long, stubborn efforts with stated national reasons, which is what makes the texts' refusal to colour effort bite. And the forest in the monsoon is a first-rate sight, the island's only lowland rainforest on the World Heritage list, filmed in the season visitors avoid.

historical_thread.story:
Most of the forest was declared a forest reserve on 3 May 1875 under the Waste Lands Ordinance (Ceylon Government Gazette No. 4046, 8 May 1875), and the rest notified a proposed reserve in the early twentieth century (IUCN Directory of South Asian Protected Areas, 1990). J. R. Baker, who camped near it in 1936, called it 'the only considerable patch of virgin tropical rain-forest in the island' (Geographical Journal, 1937). Aerial and ground surveys in the 1950s and a Colombo-Plan forest inventory in 1961 (de Rosayro; Merritt and Ranatunga; Andrews) assessed its potential for selective logging. The directory, citing Gunatilleke (1978) and the Forest Department (1986), says the reserve 'remained untouched until 1968 when a government directive was issued to extract timber for the plywood sawmill and chipwood complex established at Kosgama. From 1971 until 1977, when logging was banned, largely due to public pressure with the Wildlife and Nature Protection Society playing a leading role (see Hoffmann, 1972, 1977), about 1,400ha of forest in the western sector were selectively logged.' It records 6,500 to 7,000 ha unlogged, the Forest Department's planting of Caribbean pine along the periphery from 1978 as a live boundary, and, citing de Zoysa and Raheem (1987), that Honduran mahogany planted 'along abandoned logging trails as an enrichment species may lead to displacement of natural species, especially as it is a prolific seed producer'. It also warns that routes opened by contractors outside the reserve may make it 'more accessible to illicit timber operations'.

The campaign's side is told in Douglas B. Ranasinghe's authorised biography of Thilo Hoffmann, excerpted in The Island (11 June 2023). By that account the plywood and chipboard complex, of four million cubic feet a year, was built with Romanian aid 85 km north-west of the forest; the logging was to be done mechanically with Canadian aid; the contractors 'cleared and built from Veddagala to Sinharaja a wide road' for their equipment and lorries; and 'where the Research Station stands today there rose a machine yard and repair shop'. In September 1970 the society had agreed to the logging provided 1,000 to 1,200 acres were left undisturbed; after three days in the forest in February 1972 Hoffmann wrote in the society's booklet The Sinharaja Forest 1972 that he had believed selective logging would be 'a sensible and acceptable economical measure' and had come to 'the firm conclusion' that the reserves should be left alone. A memorandum signed by many organisations went to Prime Minister Sirimavo Bandaranaike on 18 May 1972, followed on 5 June by Hoffmann's suggestions to the Ministry of Planning for meeting the timber need, among them 'enrichment of 250,000 acres of degraded and secondary wet zone forest with mahogany'; a government committee chaired by George Rajapaksa heard evidence for years and reported (published 1976) mostly on yields and quotas; the contractors claimed regeneration in 20 years, the botanist Willem Meijer estimated 40 to 80. A 1,500-acre pilot was exceeded, and on a visit in March 1975 the society was told about 3,000 acres had been logged. The skid tracks 'were then planted with mahogany', and 'it is the area altered in this manner that is today mainly accessible to the visiting public'. After the 1977 election the new government decreed that logging should cease. Ishwaran and Erdelen (Ambio, 1990), as cited in a 2021 summary, add that the first road into the forest was built from Veddagala in 1963 as a jeep track 'for scientific explorations', and that mechanised logging begun in 1971 was abandoned in 1972, restarted on a limited scale in 1974 and abandoned in 1977.

The reserve became a biosphere reserve in April 1978; the National Heritage Wilderness Areas Act No. 3 of 1988 was certified on 4 March 1988; the reserve was notified a national heritage wilderness area on 21 October 1988 (Gazette No. 528/14, 7,648.2 ha) and inscribed on the World Heritage list in 1988 (8,864 ha). It remains the only area declared under that Act.
historical_thread.how_it_binds: C021's question is whether the working parts of purposeful action, effort above all, carry any moral colour of their own. The texts say no: they are wholly good in a good mind and wholly bad in a bad one [C021-P:L25], and effort in particular is a mental factor distinct from the bodily strength that shares its name [C021-M:L19]. This site's record asks exactly that, three times over, in documents rather than by resemblance. One road carried a scientists' track, a logging haul road and a research route. Two long campaigns of not falling back, a contract extended past its pilot and the opposition of a society that had agreed to the logging in 1970 and turned against it in 1972, each gave the nation's interest as its reason. And the planting that followed, mahogany put on the skid tracks as an 'enrichment species', is itself named in the 1990 directory as a danger; the campaign had itself proposed mahogany enrichment for degraded forest elsewhere. The Pradeepika's downhill boat and uphill load [C021-P:L53] are an image of a mind, and the record deliberately does not tell us which way any mind ran; the film's honesty depends on saying so. C005 closes the argument from the other side: the texts would sort the logging by its aim [C005-M:L5] [C005-M:L9], and a stated use in a plan is not an aim anyone can see. The question of who wrote the story down is part of the film: the fullest account is the campaigner's own authorised biography, the figures are the Forest Department's, and the logging side's committee report was reached only through the campaigner's quotations of it.
what_is_certain: Most of the area was declared a forest reserve on 3 May 1875 under the Waste Lands Ordinance and notified in Ceylon Government Gazette No. 4046 of 8 May 1875 (IUCN directory, 1990).
J. R. Baker, after a visit in 1936, described it as 'the only considerable patch of virgin tropical rain-forest in the island' (Geographical Journal 89, 1937, as quoted in the IUCN directory).

Surveys in the 1950s and the 1961 Colombo-Plan forest inventory assessed its potential for selective logging (de Rosayro 1954, 1959; Merritt and Ranatunga 1959; Andrews 1961, as listed in the IUCN directory).

A government directive of 1968 ordered timber extraction for the plywood sawmill and chipwood complex at Kosgama; logging from 1971 to 1977 selectively logged about 1,400 ha of the western sector; logging was banned in 1977, 'largely due to public pressure' with the Wildlife and Nature Protection Society leading (IUCN directory, 1990, citing Gunatilleke 1978, Forest Department 1986, Hoffmann 1972 and 1977; repeated in the UNEP-WCMC World Heritage datasheet).

The directory records 6,500 to 7,000 ha of unlogged forest, Caribbean pine planted along the periphery from 1978 as a live boundary, and Honduran mahogany planted along abandoned logging trails as an enrichment species that 'may lead to displacement of natural species' (citing de Zoysa and Raheem 1987).
Hoffmann's booklet The Sinharaja Forest (1972) and his 'Epitaph for a forest. Sinharaja - 1976' (Loris 14, 1977) are in the directory's and the WCMC datasheet's reference lists.

The reserve was recognised as a biosphere reserve in April 1978; notified a national heritage wilderness area on 21 October 1988 (Gazette No. 528/14; 18,899 acres 12 perches, 7,648.2 ha); inscribed on the World Heritage list in 1988 (8,864 ha in the nomination) (IUCN directory; WCMC datasheet).
The National Heritage Wilderness Areas Act is No. 3 of 1988, certified 4 March 1988 (CommonLII; Laws of Sri Lanka).

Kudawa is the main entrance and the Forest Department's base; the former logging road between the Kudawa base and the research station is the route most birders use (Oriental Bird Club guide; WCMC datasheet on the entrances).
Kudawa and the research-station clearing both lie in Ratnapura District (OpenStreetMap/Nominatim reverse geocoding).
what_is_disputed: The area logged. About 1,400 ha (IUCN directory 1990, citing Gunatilleke 1978 and Forest Department 1986; UNEP-WCMC datasheet; a 2021 summary citing Gunawardene et al. 2010) against about 14,000 ha (a National Trust Sri Lanka leaflet, which otherwise reproduces the directory's sentence word for word). 14,000 ha is larger than the whole reserve (8,864 ha in the nomination, 11,187 ha today) and cannot be right; it is recorded as a copying error and never used. The campaign's own count in March 1975 was about 3,000 acres (about 1,200 ha) 'possibly even more', a separate, earlier figure, kept apart.

Which aid built what. The campaigner's biography says the plywood complex was built with Romanian aid and the mechanised logging contract carried out with Canadian aid; Rohan Pethiyagoda's 2015 review of that biography in the Sunday Times says the factory itself was 'constructed using Canadian aid'. The biography's fuller account is preferred; the voice says only 'a foreign-aided logging contract'.

When logging ended. 1977 (IUCN directory; WCMC; the biography, after the 1977 election) against 'finally abandoned in 1978' (Sunday Times review, 2015). Ishwaran and Erdelen (1990), as cited, give a stop in 1972 and a restart on a limited scale in 1974 before abandonment in 1977; a 2021 summary gives the logging years as 1972 to 1977.

Why it ended. 'Public pressure' (IUCN directory), a new government's decision after the 1977 election (biography), or 'respect for this symbolic role' of the forest (WCMC datasheet, citing de Zoysa and Simon 1999). These are different kinds of cause and are not merged.

The first road. Built from Veddagala in 1963 as a jeep track 'for scientific explorations' (Ishwaran and Erdelen 1990, reached only as cited in a 2021 summary) against a wide road cleared and built by the logging contractors (the biography). Both may be true of successive stages; neither source was reached in its original.

The research-station ground. The biography says a machine yard and repair shop stood 'where the Research Station stands today'; a birding summary says the research centre once hosted the logging workshop. It could not be confirmed which building is meant (the Forest Department's Kudawa centre or the field research station further in), or from any source independent of the campaign.

The protecting law's dates in the campaigner's own words. Hoffmann (Loris, 1991, as quoted in the biography) gives the Act as 1985 and the declaration as 1989; the Act is No. 3 of 1988 and the gazette is dated 21 October 1988. The biography also quotes him saying the Forest Department made the Act to keep the forest under its control; that is an interested party's claim about an institution and is not used.
Regeneration time. The logging contractors' claim of 20 years against Willem Meijer's estimate of 40 to 80 years, both as reported in the biography only.
The 1926 watershed reserve of 9,203 ha appears in the WCMC datasheet but not in the IUCN directory; not used.

Why the skid tracks were planted with mahogany. The IUCN directory (1990) calls it planting 'as an enrichment species', a forestry term for putting valuable timber into logged forest; the biography says only that the tracks 'were then planted with mahogany, an exotic tree', and gives no planter, date or reason. No source reached says the planting was meant to repair the logging damage, and the film does not say so (corrected in audit, 2026-09-26).

When the society turned against the logging. The biography has Hoffmann warning of the threat at the 1969 AGM, a deputation in 1970 that persuaded the Forest Department to spare 1,000 to 1,200 acres, an AGM resolution in December 1971, and the decision to oppose the logging entirely only after the February 1972 visit; the Rajapaksa committee's report, as the biography quotes it, records the 1970 agreement and the later change. The voice therefore dates the opposition to 1972, not 1971.

what_to_film: The forest from outside its edge, from the road below the entrance: a long lens across tea and scrub to forested ridges under monsoon cloud, rain crossing in bands. Locked.

The old road from the entrance to the research-station clearing, in a series of locked frames each composed straight down the road's line with the vanishing point centred: the entrance stretch, a sunken stretch with water running in the ruts, a bend under closed canopy. Tripod at standing height, a normal to slightly long lens; no pans, no walking shots, no gimbal.
A band of heavy rain arriving: the sound on the canopy high up first, then the drops on the road, recorded in sync from one held frame.
A stream beside the road in spate, locked at the water's edge.
The research-station clearing from the road's last metres, rain easing, mist lifting; a mixed bird flock crossing if the break gives one.

The payoff: the one frame composed square to the roadside, on a row of planted mahogany along an old skid track, identified on the ground with the Forest Department. Held through the end of a shower until the leaves stop dripping.
Clean sound throughout: rain on canopy, drip, streams, and the forest's own sound in the breaks. No music is needed.
suggested_location.access: By road to Kudawa village via Kalawana and Weddagala, then on foot from the main (Kudawa) entrance; visitor entry is by ticket and with a Forest Department guide, and filming for a production needs a separate permit from the Forest Department, which manages the reserve under the National Heritage Wilderness Areas Act. The route along the old road to the research-station clearing is a few kilometres on foot. No drone is planned; a World Heritage forest under the Forest Department would also need Civil Aviation Authority and defence clearance for one. Leeches are heavy in the wet season; lens and sound protection from continuous rain is essential.
suggested_location.best_time: The south-west monsoon, roughly May to July (the directory gives May to July and November to January as the main rains, with February dry), in the mornings. Plan several days: bands of rain with breaks between are needed, and a mixed bird flock crossing the road at the clearing is luck.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only; no access, permit, participant or filming condition has been verified. The logging history rests on the full text of the IUCN Directory of South Asian Protected Areas (Green, 1990) read on archive.org, which cites Gunatilleke (1978), the Forest Department (1986), Hoffmann (1972, 1977) and de Zoysa and Raheem (1987), none of which was reached in the original; it is repeated in the UNEP-WCMC datasheet, whose stated principal source is the 1988 World Heritage nomination. The earliest attestation actually reached for the 1,400 ha figure is therefore 1990, resting on the Forest Department's and Gunatilleke's figures. The campaign's detail (the road, the machine yard, the 1970 agreement, the 1972 booklet and memorandum, the committee, the mahogany on the skid tracks) comes from Douglas B. Ranasinghe's authorised biography of Thilo Hoffmann as excerpted in The Island in 2023, read through the Wayback Machine; it is an interested party's account and the record says so. Ishwaran and Erdelen (Ambio 19(5), 1990) were reached only as cited in a 2021 web summary. Corrections to the blind proposal: the 14,000 ha variant is traced to a National Trust Sri Lanka leaflet copying the directory's sentence and is impossible on its own terms; the proposal's 'Romanian aid' is right for the factory but the logging contract was Canadian-aided; the proposal's 1926 reserve date is in the WCMC datasheet only. District: Kudawa and the research-station clearing reverse-geocode to Ratnapura District on OpenStreetMap; the reserve also extends into Galle and Matara, but no shot is outside Ratnapura. District budget: Ratnapura moves from 2 to 3 with this film, counting only films currently written; within the preferred band. Several GRP-02/03 slots were reopened on 2026-09-26 and may move the count. Images: Commons holds no confirmed picture of the old road or of the planted mahogany; the two files used were confirmed through the Commons API, and the road image is captioned as unconfirmed for the exact track. The payoff depends on a planted mahogany row being identifiable from the road; that has not been verified and is a drop condition. Fallback in a different district: the Kanneliya forest in Galle District, reported as logged in the 1970s and 1980s; its logging history was not confirmed and it has no comparable single road story.

unknowns: No access, permission or filming condition has been found or confirmed. Everything here is a research direction.
Whether a planted mahogany row on an old skid track is still standing and identifiable from the road, and where.
Which building the campaign's account means by the research station on the old machine-yard ground, and whether any source independent of the campaign confirms it.
The 1963 jeep track: Ishwaran and Erdelen (1990) were not reached in the original.

The government committee's report (published 1976), the 1968 directive and the 1977 order ending logging were not reached; the logging side's reasons are known only through the campaign's quotations and the directory's summary.
Whether the Forest Department will allow tripod work on the road in the monsoon.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location was proposed by Claude and awaits Chathura's review; it has not been confirmed. The logging dates and the logged area are documentary at one remove (the IUCN directory of 1990, citing the Forest Department and Gunatilleke, repeated in the WCMC datasheet); the Act's number and the gazette date are from legal databases and the directory; the campaign's account, including the road and the machine yard, is from the campaigner's authorised biography and is an interested party's; the 1963 road is secondary. The district was checked by reverse geocoding. Access, permissions and filming conditions are desk research and unverified. No scene or shot has been filmed.
